items.author: Mike Clark Director, Product Management
items.summary: For the third time in a row, Google Cloud is recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Application Development Platforms , positioned highest overall on the Ability to Execute axis. 1 These days, it’s very clear to us that organizations are looking for AI to handle actual day-to-day work, stay strictly within compliance guardrails, and deliver measurable ROI. In the last year, nearly 500 Google Cloud customers each processed more than one trillion tokens . And a lot of that volume came from heavily regulated sectors like global banking, healthcare, and telecommunications. Our customers choose Gemini because it delivers an open enterprise platform built for this level of production scale, by: Unifying the agent experience across everyday workflows Providing unrestricted model choice without vendor lock-in Practicing cost discipline before bills spiral, not after Governing agents through a single, centralized control plane 1. Gemini delivers one universal agent across the enterprise In October, we announced a unified Gemini experience. The same Gemini you collaborate with every day is now your enterprise agent to get real work done. Instead of navigating disconnected developer consoles, consumer tools, and workplace add-ons, Gemini meets work wherever it already happens – collaborating natively inside surfaces like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, internal chats, web, and mobile. You give Gemini high-level business objectives rather than step-by-step instructions, and it orchestrates the necessary tools, context, and coworker agents to deliver a finished result. As employees engage it, the agent retains persistent memory, understands your specific business language, and respects enterprise permissions across every device. When a team automates a complex procedure, they can package it into a shared skill, turning one group’s procedural knowledge into a capability anyone across the organization can use. That shared foundation is what transforms agent building from an isolated engineering backlog into an organization-wide capability. At Dojo , one of UK’s leading payment providers, non-technical teams used this exact environment to stand up over 600 custom agents in just two months: “When you can use natural language, anyone from HR to sales can turn their unique business experience into a custom AI agent in minutes. In two months, we created over 600 agents. The majority were built by our frontline business teams right inside Gemini, leaving our developers to focus on more complex challenges.” – Robert Howes, Chief Technology Officer, Dojo. Dojo fuels an AI-native future, delivers 680+ agents in two months with Gemini Dojo fuels an AI-native future, delivers 680+ agents in two months with Gemini 2. We bring the leading frontier models under one roof Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading frontier model families, from Google, Anthropic and OpenAI, on a unified enterprise platform – and across every surface, from developer tooling in Antigravity to everyday productivity in Gemini for web, mobile, and desktop. Through the model garden, organizations can access over 200 models, drawing down existing cloud commitments on a single invoice without having to negotiate separate contracts. At the same time, we are deeply proud of the pace of innovation coming out of Google DeepMind. Over the past month alone, we’ve rolled out a full generation of specialized models: Gemini 4 Argon for strong performance across complex software engineering, law, finance, and cyber defense; Gemini 4 Carbon for frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows; and now Gemini 4 Hydrogen , bringing cutting-edge intelligence with speed and efficiency to everyday coding and agentic execution. By treating models as a diversified portfolio, we give our customers the freedom to optimize for speed, precision, and cost across every task. For PayPal , this flexibility is central to their strategy: “We built a unified LLM stack. That meant we ran our open source models on top of our inferencing stack on GKE, and we ran our close-sourced models on top of the Gemini platform. Developers get choice – Claude, Gemini, Open Source – through one consistent governed access layer. That’s why we love the model garden.” — Srinivasan Manoharan, Director of AI/ML Platform, PayPal. PayPal paves the way for the future of agentic commerce with Google Cloud PayPal paves the way for the future of agentic commerce with Google Cloud 3. Optimizing spend at every layer of the stack A recurring concern we hear from enterprise leaders is the unpredictability of AI billing. When teams start scaling agents, pay-as-you-go pricing can feel like an open tab with no ceiling. That is why we optimize cost across every layer of the stack – co-designing custom TPU silicon, cluster networking, and foundation models as a single system to drive down baseline costs. At the execution level, we give finance and engineering teams the right levers to innovate without risking their margins. Gemini dynamically matches every task to the most cost-effective model, handling high-volume tasks with efficient models, only escalating to frontier reasoning models for complex problem-solving. Paired with native FinOps controls – including project-level monthly spend caps, anomaly detection, and Flexible Savings Plans – leaders get hard financial boundaries and clear visibility. For companies processing massive volumes of data, this approach makes all the difference. At Imgix , the engineering team prioritized this architectural discipline as they scaled visual processing: “If we're using the most expensive model every single time, that's going to be a big bill for our customers. So we use a cheaper model like Gemini Flash to figure out, ‘Does this image or video even need this AI feature?’ before routing further down the pipeline.” – Alfonso Acosta, Head of Engineering, Imgix. Imgix processes 8 billion daily media requests 50% faster with Google Cloud Imgix processes 8 billion daily media requests 50% faster with Google Cloud 4. A single control plane for governed enterprise context When organizations empower employees to build and deploy agents at scale, governance cannot be an afterthought. It must be an inherent part of the environment in which those agents operate. With Gemini, every agent is assigned a dedicated Agent Identity, ensuring that all database queries, tool actions, and state transitions generate an auditable record tied directly to authorized roles. Execution occurs inside isolated runtime sandboxes, where Agent Gateway and Model Armor automatically scrub sensitive data, block policy violations, and enforce corporate compliance in real time. That same control plane extends to how agents interact with corporate intelligence. Rather than requiring organizations to move, replicate, or duplicate sensitive records into yet another external repository, Gemini connects directly to live enterprise systems. Agents ground their reasoning in data across BigQuery, Cloud Storage, SAP, Salesforce, S3, and Azure – inheriting existing user access controls and keeping proprietary data strictly within its original perimeter. Governed context and centralized control are what make company-wide agent adoption possible. UKG relied on Gemini’s security, governance, and evaluation controls to skip building that foundation from scratch: “The Gemini platform, it’s solving some of these key problems that we already were trying to solve — from hosting agents to securing them to the governance around them, evals to make sure they’re behaving correctly. I can just use these things out of the box and get back to creating value.” – Thomas Newton, Head of Cloud and Engineering, UKG. By combining frontier intelligence, universal agent orchestration across everyday tools, predictable economics, and enterprise governance, Gemini gives developers and business leaders the foundation to build with velocity and operate with confidence. items.title: Introducing eve 1.0
items.author: Andrew Barba
items.summary: Today we're announcing eve 1.0 , the open-source framework for building production-ready agents. Since the public preview in June , we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available. We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite. With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead. Build production agents on a harness you own The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in. For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation. Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product. Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week. Lindy 's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”. Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team. In the native Slack channel , each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack. Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn. Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list. Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately. The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components. Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI. Build multi-tenant agents One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules. Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory , connection credentials , and approval policy for that tenant and user. Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions. Give agents memory across sessions We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself . Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel. Other providers include claude-mem , Hindsight , Kybernesis Arcana , Memanto , memco , Supermemory , and Upstash AgentKit . Trace agents with OpenTelemetry We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry , so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself. Tracing integrations include Raindrop , with more options in the integrations directory . Add one with eve add instrumentation/ , or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration. Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents. You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls. On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration. Lower agent turn latency At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn . In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms . The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response. Hosted stress run Median turn latency p95 September 1, beta baseline 3.036s 3.692s November 15, 1.0.0 414ms 633ms We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9 , which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK. eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner. Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. We've also cut repeated work in workflow steps, checkpoints, and sandbox setup: Workflow steps save changes and refer back to data already stored, instead of repeatedly copying a growing conversation into each step. Steps that don't need history no longer receive it. Checkpoints store references to image files returned by tools, so they don't have to copy the image bytes each time. Sandboxes from prepared snapshots skip repeated setup. Stop a sandbox and keep its files for reuse. Cleanup starts when the session ends. The storage changes are part of the open-source Workflow SDK, so agents you host yourself on other Workflow backends also store less duplicate session data. The cost estimate above uses Vercel Workflows pricing . On Vercel, workflow steps run on Fluid compute . They need extra storage writes for inputs above the payload size limit, so sending less session data helps keep turn times consistent as sessions grow. Images and files can still require those writes. For model calls, tool and skill listings can stay out of the initial prompt until they're needed. Connection tools run through eve__search and eve__tool , so each search no longer has to expand the model's tool list. We also changed how eve marks parts of a prompt for provider caching, so more content can be reused between calls. During an earlier migration to eve, an engineer at Evisions reported: Share agent capabilities with extensions Since the preview, we've added extensions so teams can share tools, skills, instructions, connections, channels, schedules, hooks, and subagents without copying files between agents. You can use extensions from the extensions directory or create your own with npx eve@latest extension init . For example, agent-browser adds browser automation, Mux Video adds tools for video assets and clips, and Link adds wallet and purchase tools. eve builds workspace extensions from source and reloads changes during development. You can update shared capabilities in one package and try the changes in your agents as you work. Build coding agents with eve’s shared tools The 1.0 code extension builds on eve’s default file tools, adding coding instructions and skills that follow your repository’s AGENTS.md . It's included in the eve package, so there's nothing extra to install. Give it a repository in its sandbox and your agent can investigate code, edit files, and run the project's checks. It uses the same harness and extension system as your other agents, so you can replace or disable tools, override skills, and add your own instructions. See the benchmark results for comparisons with other coding harnesses using the same tasks and model. Add the coding extension to your agent: The companion eve/extensions/git adds GitHub and pull request workflows, using credentials and authorization you configure. On Vercel, the optional remote self-modification extension lets your agent propose changes to its own source in a draft pull request. You review the changes, merge them, and deploy. Build with the same public APIs eve uses We built eve's subagents, sleep, and question tools on the same workflow system you can use through defineWorkflowTool . Your tools can return a result, start a background task, or keep accepting messages as a resumable task. They can wait for a person, webhook, or timer without keeping compute running, and their runs survive restarts. You don't need a separate background-job system to coordinate that work. Once you've defined a reviewer subagent, this tool returns a receipt immediately. The task body waits for the reviewer's result, which is delivered to the model in a later message: Upgrade to eve 1.0 If you already have an eve agent, the 1.0 upgrade guide walks through the changes to extension builds, agent APIs, session events, clients, and saved history. Follow it before deploying your upgrade. eve follows semantic versioning , so breaking changes to stable APIs only happen in major releases. Experimental and internal APIs, including experimental fields, can change between major releases. To work through the upgrade with your coding agent, copy this prompt: Create your first eve agent Start in the terminal to build locally, use the browser builder to create and deploy an agent, or choose a template for your use case. Start in the terminal Create a new agent from the CLI with Node.js 24 or newer: In an interactive terminal, this installs dependencies and opens the eve terminal UI. If your selected team has AI Gateway access, you can start chatting without creating a Vercel project or copying an API key. eve can use your existing Vercel CLI credentials to call models through AI Gateway locally. Use /login to sign in to other connections. In eve dev , you can ask the agent to add a tool, change its instructions, or write a skill. With self-modification , it edits its own source and reloads the change for the next turn. Start in the browser From the Vercel dashboard, the agent builder scaffolds an agent, creates its Git repo, and deploys it. Go to Add New → Agent, pick a model, and add web chat or Slack along the way. Start from a template Choose an eve template for your use case: Use case Templates Coding Coding agent · Software factory · GitHub maintainer · Incident response Knowledge and data Company brain · Data analyst · Shared files with Vercel Drives Apps and interfaces Next.js chat · TanStack Start chat · Voice agent · Agent with Python Messaging Slack · Discord · Personal agent · BELL Stack Memory Memory agent · Mem0 Content and marketing Contentful · Sanity copilot · Content agent · Marketing team Learn more in the eve docs . items.title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
items.author: Roman Gushchin Software Engineer, AI & Infrastructure
items.summary:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load. Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs. To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko , an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year. In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild. Reviewing code is hard Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code. To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative: LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence. LLMs are easier to bias . The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes. How Sashiko reviews a patch To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs , and requires each pass to record what it ruled out: code_block Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)
 -> Triage
 -> Per-bug deep checks
 -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', )])]> Notes on each step: Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list. All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev . Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code. What the data shows The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions. It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle. It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization. Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic. Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%. A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch. This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch: "As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds ( on lore.kernel.org ) Sashiko at a glance Since March 2026 Patch reviews completed 241,000 (~1200+ / day) Opted-in kernel subsystem lists 75+ Mainline commits crediting Sashiko 2,000+ 2026 Linux kernel CVEs crediting Sashiko 528 60-day post-merge fix rate Down from 3.4% baseline to 2.2% (Linux 7.2) What we learned from building and running Sashiko First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level). Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced. Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning , Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers. More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration. Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git. "Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev , or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.

items.title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
items.author: George Fahmy
items.summary: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done. Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery , Selection , Access , and Success . You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly. That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one. The agentic testing pyramid If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid , the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite. To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success , that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome. An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench , are E2E evals. Example Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans . Here’s a typical request from one of your customers: Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission. Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am: Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature) 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget) Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time) Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three) Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans : How to build an end-to-end eval We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor , an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions. Here are the terms we’ll use: Task : one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded Variant : the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills Trial : one attempt by one variant at one task Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output Step 1: Set a goal Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier ). Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places: Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate For example, your goal might be to: Increase the success rate on a specific task Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it A/B test a prompt Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why Example We looked in all three places for sfbeans : Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness. Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added. Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn. That gives us our goal: Goal Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for Agents Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from. In scope Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans . Out of scope Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later. Done when Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time. Step 2: Define metrics Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals: Success Success rate: the share of trials that pass Pass@k : the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”) Pass^k : the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”) Efficiency (measured on successful trials only) Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task Time: how long the trial took Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars Example Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ( anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway ) on the iced latte order could look like: Trial Result What happened Steps Time Cost 1 Pass Compared quotes from 3 cafes, ordered at Valencia 9 3:40 $0.52 2 Fail: over budget Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27 5 1:50 $0.31 3 Pass Compared quotes from 4 cafes, ordered at Valencia 11 4:30 $0.68 4 Fail: late Ordered at Dolores, ready 9:20 6 2:10 $0.35 5 Pass Skipped Fog City, ordered at Valencia 8 3:20 $0.49 What the numbers mean: Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%. Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once. Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right. Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials. Time: ~3:50 on successful trials. Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too. So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time . Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5. Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters: Product What a failed attempt costs the user Metric to lead with Order my morning coffee Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust Pass^k Coding agent with a test suite Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again Pass@k Draft an email the user reviews A quick edit before hitting send Success rate Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.” Step 3: Design the task set In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for. Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act. For each task, define these parts: An instruction: the user’s request An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent. Example We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/ . Common case: iced-latte-mission , the order from earlier Edge case: usual-unavailable , where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink Edge case: team-order , with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot Don’t act: impossible-request , where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5). Here’s iced-latte-mission : The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection , keeping the eval focused on Success . We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time: The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning: To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly. For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json : The actual check lives in check_orders.py . It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score: The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works: Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5: Step 4: Run the eval If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each. Harbor’s Vercel integration , which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox , and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers. Example Two agents, Claude Code and Codex , with two models each, make four variants. Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job: This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 ( Sandbox limits ). To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway. Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment. Step 5: Analyze traces Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied. Example The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/ . Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed: Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative). For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally. Variant Success Pass^5 Avg steps (successful) Cost per success (incl. failed trials) Claude Code + Opus 5.5 85% 60% 9 $0.61 Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 75% 52% 11 $0.27 Codex + GPT-6 Astra 80% 43% 8 $0.48 Codex + GPT-6.1 Sol 65% 14% 13 $0.22 That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials. Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke: Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json . The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order . No quote . It treated the menu price as the final price. Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money. We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.” When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring: Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO. Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one. Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins. Automated trace analysis For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it. Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs. Model calls go through AI Gateway . Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage. Iterate to greatness Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it. Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship. Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it. Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next. Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again . Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace. items.title: Agentic engineering with GitLab and your local agent: A walkthrough
items.author: John Coghlan https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/john-coghlan/
items.summary: You can build an agentic engineering environment to drive greater automation throughout your workflow. How? Start in the harness you already use and connect to GitLab Duo Agent Platform once with a skill. Longer, repository-aware workflows run on GitLab, and every merge request still hits the same reviews, pipelines, scans, and approval policies. In this article, we will show you how to quickly get started, from setup to tackling four key use cases. We focus on Claude Code as the local harness because that’s what we see most of our customers using but this same flow can apply to the local harness of your choosing, including Duo CLI . How to configure your agentic engineering environment If you already do most of your coding in a local harness, keep working there and wire it to GitLab Duo Agent Platform. From the terminal, you can direct lifecycle work to agentic workflows that run inside GitLab: Picking up an issue and opening a merge request Reviewing every MR as it lands Resolving merge conflicts Repairing a pipeline that just failed With GitLab Ultimate, triaging and fixing security findings once code lands Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and others become the place from where you direct that work. Part 1 is the setup Install the GitLab Duo setup skill , ask Claude Code to run it, and it sets up your whole top-level group with the necessary settings, the flows, an automation in every project, and the MCP connection. Part 2 walks through four workflows You can try them as soon as the setup is done, each driven from Claude Code: Find an issue assigned to you and hand it to the Developer flow. Get automated code reviews on your merge requests, act on the findings without leaving your harness, and resolve any conflicts that pop up. Use an automation to fix a failed pipeline. On Ultimate, triage and fix security findings with the security flows. When you want an even tighter loop The MR followup skill guides your local harness through the steps above even faster. The skill helps local agents monitor progress on the repo-side and take actions on your behalf to speed things along. What you need before you start A GitLab.com top-level group with GitLab Credits (Premium and Ultimate groups get access to promotional free credits each month for each user). The security workflow in Use Case 4 requires Ultimate licensing for your GitLab instance. A project in that group with a pipeline, a few open issues, and an open merge request or two, so the workflows have something to act on. The Owner role on the top-level group, so the skill can set up the whole group. If you're a Maintainer on the project but not a group owner, the skill sets up just that project and lists what to ask your Owner. Claude Code installed and signed in, plus git and the GitLab CLI (glab, signed in with glab auth login ), which the skill uses to read and change settings. Part 1: Guided setup with a skill The GitLab Duo setup skill accelerates the connection from inside your harness. You install the skill once, ask Claude Code to set up GitLab Duo. The skill sets up your group as it turns on group-wide Duo Agent Platform workflows, creates the Fix CI/CD Pipeline automation where needed, connects to GitLab MCP server , and reports anything left for you to finish. Install the skill git clone https://gitlab.com/gitlab-da/projects/agentic-eng-config.git cp -R agentic-eng-config/skills/gitlab-duo-setup ~/.claude/skills/ cp -R agentic-eng-config/skills/gitlab-mr-followup ~/.claude/skills/ Then Claude Code picks it up in the running session. If it isn't listed, restart Claude Code. You can add the skill to .claude/skills/ inside the repo so teammates can use it too. Run the skill In your project directory, start Claude Code and invoke the skill with a slash command: /gitlab-duo-setup Note: Different harnesses can have a different syntax for invoking skills. What happens Before it changes anything, the skill reads your top-level group and its projects and shows you one plan: every change and what it covers (the groups or projects). Group changes reach every downstream project and every member, and the plan says so. It waits for your yes, and you can drop any line. Then it: Turns on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and flow execution for the group, and adds the Code Review , Duo Developer , and Fix CI/CD Pipeline flows to the group's flows. Flows you already have stay on. Turns on automatic code review for the group, which carries down to every project. Creates an automation in every project with CI/CD that runs Fix CI/CD Pipeline when a pipeline fails. Projects that already have one are skipped, so running the skill twice is safe. Adds the GitLab MCP server to Claude Code, user-level or project-level as you prefer, and walks you through signing in in the browser. Verifies by calling list_duo_agents_and_flows . A successful call proves the sign-in worked, and the flows it returns prove the settings took. On Ultimate, asks one optional question: Do you also want GitLab to triage and fix security findings? Say "yes" and Use Case 4 will cover what gets turned on. Say "no" and the setup is done. Ends with a short report and links for anything it couldn't do. Blockers may be runners, if a project has none that can run flows, or push rules, if your group enforces them. Why use a skill for setup A skill sets things up in the same place you already direct agent work. You stay in your preferred coding harness, approve a plan, and wire Duo Agent Platform for group-wide automation without breaking out of that loop. It's also harness-neutral by design (the repo's AGENTS.md requires it), so the same skill works whether your team is on Claude Code today and something else next quarter. If the GitLab tools don't show up Run /mcp and check that GitLab shows as connected. Connected but no tools? Restart Claude Code; new servers load at session start. A 403 when you sign in usually means MCP client access is off for your top-level group: A group Owner turns on Allow connection to GitLab under the group's Settings > General > Permissions and group features . If two GitLab entries, user and project scope, show duplicate tools, keep one. Part 2: Four workflows, all run from your terminal With the GitLab MCP server connected in Part 1, Claude Code can now find your issues, start a flow, read review threads and pipeline status, and reply on a thread over that single OAuth connection. Server instructions help Claude Code propose the right agentic workflow within Duo Agent Platform, and each call comes with an AI audit event for your platform team. The agent reads issues and merge request context through these tools, allowing the coding harness to access GitLab artifacts you trust. Use Case 1: Hand an issue to the Developer flow The first thing most people want from an agent is simple: Take the issue I was assigned this morning and come back with a merge request. Find the work In Claude Code, ask something like: ? Summarize each in a line. " language="unset" meta="" style=""> What issues are assigned to me in ? Summarize each in a line. Claude calls the GitLab MCP server's work item tools, filters your assignments, and gives you the list. You pick one. If the issue is thin, this is also where you'd ask Claude to read the linked files or recent commits through the repository tools so you can sharpen the description before handing it off; a clearer goal produces a better MR. Hand it off Ask Claude to assign the Developer flow to an issue. Can you pick up Issue 1 and assign it to the Developer flow in GitLab? Claude calls the server's Start Duo session tool with the project, the Developer flow, and a goal it writes from the issue, and hands you back a session link. From here the work happens in GitLab, not on your machine. This frees you up to keep working locally without disrupting the agent. The session runs as a CI job on a runner. The flow reads the issue and the repository, writes the change, and opens a merge request. The MR is attributed to you, not to the service account, so it shows up in your activity and your review queue like any other MR you authored. Use Case 2: Automated code review From the harness, open or push an MR and let Duo Agent Platform review it on GitLab. You read findings and iterate locally while the review and verification stay on the merge request. GitLab Code Review flow reviews every merge request in your group as soon as the MR is marked ready. Once turned on, it enables agentic reviews and approvals. On new groups and projects, Code Review flow is on by default, so those features are active out of the box. On existing groups and projects, you can run the setup skill to turn it on. To check or change it for one project, go to Settings > Merge requests > GitLab Duo Code Review > Enable automatic reviews by GitLab Duo . There you can also choose to Start a new review on push so every commit to the MR branch gets a follow-up review that builds on the earlier one. What a review looks like When you or your agent creates an MR, GitLab Duo is added as a reviewer and runs a two-stage review: a pre-scan that pulls related files, tests and dependencies from the repo, then the review itself. It leaves inline threads with specific, actionable findings plus a summary. With the beta approvals setting (also on the project's Merge requests settings page) turned on, GitLab Duo approves the MR when it finds nothing or requests changes when it does. Tune it for your repo Two files let you shape reviews without touching settings: mr-review-instructions.yaml for custom review instructions (focus areas, standards, per-path rules) and .gitlab/duo/mr-review-automated-rules.yaml to exclude MRs by target branch, source branch, or author, for example, bot-authored dependency bumps. As you identify improvements, keep updating these instructions to make reviews more efficient over time. Work the feedback locally Ask your agent: Does MR 1 have feedback for me to review? Claude Code reads Duo's Code Review threads through the MCP Server and summarizes them for you. You can ask it to follow through by fixing the ones it agrees with and reply in the threads to resolve them. Claude will make those changes locally, push them, and comment on each thread as the user. If you have the start a new review on push setting turned on, Duo will run another review to verify those changes. If a finding comes with a code suggestion, you can apply via MCP. Long-running agentic work and verification stay on the merge request. Quick iteration stays in your local checkout. Resolve a merge conflict While a merge request waits for review, its target branch keeps moving. Eventually, this can lead to a conflict on your branch. You can clear it from Claude Code in two ways. Let Claude resolve it in your checkout: MR 1 conflicts with its target branch. Resolve the conflict and get the pipeline green. Or hand it over to Duo Developer on GitLab: MR 1 has a merge conflict. Can you ask the Developer flow in GitLab to resolve it? If you use Claude Code to resolve it, it will go through the conflict locally and use any preferences in your Agents.MD or skills to resolve it. If you use GitLab Duo Developer flow, you can leave it to work on it within your GitLab instance and move on to your next task. Use Case 3: Fix a failed pipeline with an automation From the harness you can watch the merge request, while Duo Agent Platform can start the automated Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow when a job fails, with the same repo context and merge gates as any other change. An automation watches for a failed pipeline and starts the Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow for you. By the time you notice the pipeline failure, a fix is usually already waiting. Check the automation Automations live at AI > Automations in each project. If you ran the skill, the fixed pipeline automation will already be there, along with some other automations that come out of the box. To create one by hand (Maintainer or Owner): Select New automation and give it a name, for example Fix failed pipelines . Under Runs with , select Fix CI/CD Pipeline . (Developer is selected by default if it's enabled; change it.) Under Runs when , select Add trigger > On an event , choose Pipeline events , and under Run when select Failed . Select Add event , then Create . What happens on a failure When a pipeline fails, the flow starts a session. If the pipeline belongs to an open merge request, it posts a system note on the MR with a link to the session. It reads the job logs, the MR diff, and the repository, then: If the fix is inside the MR's diff, it applies inline code suggestions on the source branch. You review and apply them from the MR, or pull the branch and apply them locally. If the fix needs files outside the diff, or the pipeline has no open MR, it opens a new merge request with the change. If it can't determine a reliable fix, or the failure is security-sensitive, it posts a comment that describes the failure and next steps so you can decide how to proceed. Make it fit your project The flow reads AGENTS.md, so you can tell it how to format commit messages, which labels to put on MRs it opens, how to treat specific failure classes, and when to stop retrying the same fix. One known limit: The flow sees only the last 150 KiB of a job log, so noisy jobs may need a summary step at the end. Close the loop from Claude Code The flow leaves a system note and its suggestions on the MR, so start from the MR. On MR 17, did Fix Pipeline create a new MR or leave suggestions? Show me the diff and the reasoning. Decide whether to merge the MR or apply the suggestions. The MR followup skill can also help you take the MR all the way to merge and guide you through the process. /gitlab-mr-followup Take MR 1 through to merge. Use Case 4: Triage and fix security findings (Ultimate) For GitLab Ultimate + Duo Agent Platform users, three out-of-the-box agents can also help eliminate security debt that builds up once code lands: Secret False Positive Detection , SAST False Positive Detection , and Resolve SAST Vulnerability . These security flows take findings from your scanners, score them for false positives, and open merge requests that fix the real ones. The flows work on findings from scans of your default branch (and other tracked branches), after code has merged. Turn it on If you said yes to the setup skill's security question, the skill then: Adds the SAST False Positive Detection, Secret Detection False Positive Detection, and Resolve SAST Vulnerability flows to the group, keeping every flow you already have. Applies the Secret Detection and SAST scan profile to projects that don't scan yet, without editing any .gitlab-ci.yml . The scans run in merge request pipelines, so if your tests only run in branch pipelines, check that a failing test still blocks the merge request. Enables the flows to run the Standard preset: triage and fixes run automatically after every scan, for Medium findings and above, with up to 15 open fix merge requests per project. If anything in this step fails, the skill stops there and leaves the setup from Part 1 as it is. Credits scale with the number of findings, so if you'd rather see results and cost first, ask for the Conservative preset when the skill shows its plan: on demand, for High and Critical findings, with at most five open fix merge requests. Automated resolution out-of-the-box After turning these on, agents will flag SAST and Secrets false positives for you and generate merge requests to address SAST vulnerabilities automatically, reducing your time spent on security. Expect triage and the first fix MR about 10 minutes after the scan finishes. The Security Review flow and the Vulnerability Context flow can help you dig deeper into findings that aren’t automatically addressed. Review before you merge Treat the agent-created MRs like any other. You can use the Code Review flow on the fix MRs too. Security Review, which reviews merge request changes for business logic vulnerabilities, is also available. The skill mentions it but sets it up only if you ask, because it needs experiment and beta features turned on for the whole group. Take your agentic engineering to the next level Advanced governance, flexible model deployment, and comprehensive lifecycle context ensure your automated software factory remains secure, adaptable, and fully informed. Governance that applies to every merge request To ensure control and compliance as agents take on writing more code, it’s important to build guardrails that live alongside your code. Merge request approval policies , pipeline execution policies , composite identity , and tool approval guardrails apply to agent-authored changes the same way they apply to yours. Model and cloud choice that stays under your control GitLab Duo Agent Platform is cloud-, agent-, and model-neutral. Group owners choose the model for each agent and flow, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and open-weight providers, and can update it as new models arrive. On GitLab Self-Managed, GitLab Duo Self-Hosted runs models through Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, or the organization’s own infrastructure. Lifecycle context that cuts agent retries An agent working one merge request sees only that merge request: the diff, the failing job log, and the review comments. It can't see that the same job fails in other projects. It can't see which services depend on the code it just changed, or who owns them. Without the full lifecycle picture, agents guess, then retry, then burn tokens on work that never ships. GitLab Orbit , now generally available, is a context graph of the software lifecycle. It connects code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with your permissions intact. Agents get that context before they call a change safe to merge. Developers and agents can also see which services, jobs, and environments a change touches across the group. In GitLab's internal testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries while discovering an answer, and used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible agents connect to Orbit through MCP or the GitLab CLI, so the context you build once serves every agent you add. From the same terminal, they can turn issues into merge requests, get automated review on every MR, clear merge conflicts, let a failed pipeline start its own fix, and clear their security backlog. Every change still hits the same identity, policy, CI pipelines, security, approvals, and audit rules that their organization already trusts. The GitLab Duo setup skill is how that connection starts. Install it in your harness, invoke it once, and review a single plan before anything changes. After you approve, the skill turns on Duo Agent Platform for your group, adds the Code Review, Fix CI/CD Pipeline, and Developer flows, creates the failed-pipeline automation where it is needed, connects the GitLab MCP server, and verifies the sign-in. It ends with a short report and links for anything left for you or your group Owner. From there, the four workflows in this guide run from the same terminal, and the MR followup skill is available when you want the loop even tighter. New to GitLab Duo Agent Platform? Start a free trial . Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription . Then clone the GitLab Duo setup skill , run it from the harness you already use, and take the first workflow for a spin on a real project.

items.title: Turn Slack conversations into trusted software, faster
items.author: Rebecca Carter https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/rebecca-carter/
items.summary: Most software starts as a conversation: a customer requests a new capability, a product manager weighs it against the roadmap, an engineer checks feasibility, and a security lead asks what it touches. Then someone has to turn it into work. They reread the thread, retype the decisions into an issue, and hope they didn’t miss an important detail buried in a reply. The conversation moves fast; the handoff between both teams and tools is where it slows. AI agents are uniquely equipped for that handoff: reading a long, many-voiced discussion and turning it into structured work. That leaves people free to collaborate while agents produce the output. GitLab for Slack now adds agentic capabilities and is generally available for GitLab.com users in GitLab 19.6, with support for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated to follow. Mention @GitLab in a thread in your team's channels, and the agent reads the conversation, finds what already exists, turns decisions into tracked work, and starts the agent flows that carry it to production. Work starts in Slack and lands in GitLab, where it's governed, tracked, and delivered. "Teams make decisions in Slack every day, and the best agents are the ones that can act on that context. GitLab for Slack lets agents read the conversation, take action across the software lifecycle in GitLab, and bring the results back to the thread. Teams can go from a quick discussion to planned, reviewed, and shipped work without switching tools." – Katie Steigman, Vice President Product Management, Slack Slack is the front door, GitLab does the work GitLab for Slack connects the interface where your team discusses the work to the platform where your software ships. Your team’s conversation in Slack itself becomes the agent's input, so no decision gets lost between the thread and the first commit. The agent also looks beyond the thread. When you mention @GitLab, it can read the messages in the channel where you mentioned it, so its response reflects the whole discussion and not only the replies under one message. You can also ask it to catch you up first, for example: “@GitLab, summarize #channel for me.” It works in both directions. GitLab context (what's been built, what's tracked, whether a merge request is ready, etc.) also shows up in the conversation. The conversation becomes issues, merge requests, and running agent flows, with results posted back to the thread. If your team already uses the GitLab for Slack app on GitLab.com, reinstall it today to add these agent capabilities. There's nothing new to learn; you just mention @GitLab. Use it where your team works Debate it in the channel. Draft it in your DM. GitLab for Slack works in both places: Public and private channels: Bring the agent into team discussions and turn decisions into tracked work where everyone can see it. Your own DM: Get a private space to ask questions, check on a merge request, or draft an issue before you share anything with the team. One thread, every role GitLab for Slack works for everyone who shapes the work, including people who never write code: Product managers turn a decision into scoped work before the meeting ends. Designers send their notes straight to the people and agents doing the work. Sales and customer teams bring a customer request into a team channel and follow it to production. Security and platform teams confirm agent work passes review before it ships. Engineers check what exists before building it again, without leaving the conversation. Watch GitLab for Slack in action: Governed from the first mention An agent that acts from a chat thread is only useful if you can trust what it does. The conversation happens in Slack; the work and every control stay in GitLab. Agents act only when asked. In channels, GitLab acts only when someone mentions @GitLab. In your own DM, it answers you and only you. Internal conversations only. GitLab for Slack doesn't run in external (Slack Connect) channels, so project context isn't exposed to people outside your organization. Requests run as you. Each request uses the requester's linked GitLab account, scoped to their existing permissions. If you don't have access to a project in GitLab, the agent can't access it for you in Slack. Context stays in scope. The agent reads the surrounding context only from the channel where it was mentioned. Anything it does in GitLab still follows your permissions. Actions are on the record. Each request creates an agent session in GitLab. Merge requests go through the same reviews, approval rules, and audit trail as any other change. Costs stay visible. Usage draws from your GitLab Credits, so admins can track and cap it like any other agent work. This is the model behind GitLab's governed software factory: agents speed up the work, and source control, security, and governance keep it trustworthy. Slack is one more way into that factory, not a way around it. Get started GitLab for Slack is now generally available on GitLab.com — just reinstall the GitLab for Slack app to get the new capabilities. Support for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated will follow in an upcoming release. Help us shape what's next We have a lot more planned for GitLab for Slack, and we want your feedback to guide it. Every agent response in Slack includes a thumbs up/down button, so you can tell us what worked and what didn't without leaving the thread.
